biography.text: Usha Sanyal’s 1998 article and 2005 monograph place Ahmad Riza Khan (1856–1921) in the learned society of late-nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century North India. Sanyal describes his father, Naqi Ali Khan, as his most important teacher; Khan studied the Dars-i Nizami syllabus at home and was known by the 1880s for rational sciences (maʿqulat), including logic, mathematics, and Islamic law. The monograph reports his Qadiri discipleship in 1877, pilgrimage with his father in 1878, and early fatwa-writing, while treating devotional childhood stories through their later biographical sources. His scholarly and Sufi roles coexisted; fatwa-writing was central to his career. In a first-person preface to the later Fatawa collection, he says his father assigned him fatwa work before age fourteen; searchable copies disagree on the Hijri year numeral, so the exact date remains open. Exact day-level dates and many biographical details still require primary-source review.
gaps: Collate the cited passages in Zafar ud-Din Bihari’s Urdu biography and other early records; distinguish contemporary documentation from devotional narrative.
Verify exact birth/death dates and separate year-level evidence from later day-level dates.

timeline.text: The academic biography gives year-level life dates, Qadiri discipleship in 1877, pilgrimage in 1878, the 1900 Patna honorific episode, the founding of Madrasa Manzar al-Islam in 1904, a second pilgrimage in 1905–06, and publication of Kanz al-Iman in Muradabad in 1911, reported in both Sanyal’s monograph and her Encyclopaedia of the Qur’an entry (not independent sources). Siddiqui lists four astronomy-related works dated 1919, 1920, 1920, and 1921. For Fauz-i-Mubin, introductory matter in a 2005 English rendering reports 1919 while Siddiqui lists 1920; the original Urdu imprint remains unchecked.
gaps: Inspect Urdu first editions' title pages, colophons, and any magazine antecedents to distinguish composition, serial publication, and book publication dates.

fields.text: The evidence identifies four writings associated by Siddiqui with the 1919 planetary-alignment episode: Muʿīn-i-Mubīn, Fauz-i-Mubin, al-Kalimah al-Mulhamah, and Nuzūl-i-Āyāt-i-Furqān. Sanyal independently characterizes Khan as learned in rational sciences, including logic and mathematics, but does not assess these astronomy treatises. The detailed passage study here covers only the reported preface and a geometric argument in Fauz-i-Mubin. A secondary Arabic biographical inventory also reports twenty manuscript titles across rational-science fields; the titles are cataloguing leads only, not independently verified editions or interpreted works. The dossier records historical claims; it does not validate the physical reasoning or present a stationary-Earth conclusion as modern astronomy.
gaps: Collate the Urdu originals with the cited translations and record printed Urdu pages, diagrams, and technical terminology.
Reconstruct selected arguments from original diagrams and proofs; distinguish mathematical premises from physical inferences.
Read the 2026 Urdu study on mathematical works before summarizing its abstract claims.
Check the 1919 newspapers cited by Siddiqui and independently calculate the planetary configuration before assessing the Porta episode.

legacy.text: Sanyal situates Khan’s legal and Sufi leadership in the Ahl-e Sunnat movement and wider colonial-era North Indian scholarly milieu. The research bibliography now records both Kanz al-Iman and the later Fatawa-e Rizwiyya collection, with Sanyal’s caveat that the fatwa collection is partial and its editorial history complex. Siddiqui’s four-work astronomy sequence remains introductory; the historical record here is not an assessment of scientific correctness, originality, or priority.
gaps: Review independent scholarship and the 2026 Urdu mathematical study; inspect editions, reception, and calculations with qualified historical and scientific review.
Build a complete work catalogue from library catalogues and edition title pages; current evidence is not exhaustive.

investigations.title: The argument structure of Fauz-i-Mubin and its reported geometric reasoning
investigations.field: History of astronomy / history of science in South Asia
investigations.historicalProblem: What does the available evidence establish about the structure and mathematical style of Fauz-i-Mubin, and what remains unverified until the Urdu text is examined?
investigations.historicalContext: Siddiqui situates the work amid early twentieth-century debates over Earth's motion and reports that a 1919 planetary-alignment prediction prompted a series of writings by Ahmad Raza Khan. His paper describes the work as a polemical response drawing on contemporary scientific vocabulary, geometry, logic, and religious sources. The newspaper story, chronology, and the work's arguments must be independently checked rather than taken from a sympathetic introduction as settled fact.
investigations.method: Read Siddiqui's complete article and inspected the referenced 2005 English rendering's edition matter and cited passage locator. Checked Rekhta's catalogue metadata for an Urdu-language 197-page copy contributed by Rampur Raza Library, but its page images were gated after the free allowance. Recorded Siddiqui's translations as mediated quotations; did not transcribe or translate Urdu, reconstruct the diagram, test the physical claims, or independently verify the 1919 newspaper reports.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: The author-preface excerpt as quoted by Siddiqui divides the arguments into 12, 50, and 43 items, whose stated total is 105. A later translated excerpt uses equal segments and comparisons of distances in a geometric diagram, then draws a physical inference about attraction, repulsion, and Earth's motion. Only the count sum was arithmetically checked; the geometry, translation, and physical inference were not independently tested.
investigations.reportedResult: The available evidence supports a source-linked description of how one 2023 article reports the treatise's self-described structure and one translated geometric argument. It does not establish the original edition date, the exact Urdu wording, the soundness of the calculations, or the truth of the work's stationary-Earth conclusion.
investigations.whatWasNew: This dossier converts a weakly documented catalogue entry into a reviewable research record with distinct mediation, edition, and evidence limits. It does not promote devotional claims, article praise, the author's own priority statements, or historical conclusions into verified scientific findings.
investigations.limitations: Only one academic article was read; its author says detailed analysis of the astronomical works is outside the article's primary focus. The 2005 English edition is community-produced and has unverified front-matter claims. Rekhta's Urdu pages were inaccessible after a registration gate, so no direct Urdu collation was possible. First-edition date, newspaper sources, calculation accuracy, diagram interpretation, biography, and independent reception remain open. Earth's motion is treated here only as a historical debate topic, not as a live scientific controversy.
investigations.laterInfluence: Not assessed. No transmission, scholarly reception, or influence claim is made from the source material consulted in this bounded batch.

claims.text: Siddiqui gives Ahmad Riza Khan's birth year as 1856 and birthplace as Bareilly; Sanyal independently places his life in 1856–1921 and contextualizes his role in North Indian Muslim scholarship.
claims.uncertainty: Both are secondary accounts; Sanyal gives year-level dates, not exact birth or death dates.

claims.text: Sanyal describes Ahmad Riza Khan as born in 1856 into a well-to-do, learned Pathan family in Bareilly and situates him in the intellectual climate of North India before and after the 1857 revolt.
claims.uncertainty: This is a historian's contextual summary, not a primary family record.

claims.text: Sanyal reports that Ahmad Riza Khan was educated at home by his father, Maulana Naqi Ali Khan.
claims.uncertainty: A full chronology of his teachers and curriculum remains to be established from biographical and educational sources.

claims.text: Sanyal writes that by the 1880s Ahmad Riza was known among North Indian ulama as a gifted scholar with an intellectual bent toward rational sciences including logic, mathematics, and Islamic law.
claims.uncertainty: This supports historical context and scholarly reputation, not the correctness or originality of specific mathematical calculations.

claims.text: Sanyal identifies fatwa-writing as Ahmad Riza Khan's single most important scholarly activity and a primary means by which he established his reputation and influence.
claims.uncertainty: The full fatwa corpus and its publication history are outside this focused pass.

claims.text: Siddiqui states that detailed analysis of Ahmad Raza Khan's astronomical work is not the article's primary focus.
claims.uncertainty: This reports the article's explicit scope statement.

claims.text: Siddiqui lists four related astronomy writings: Muʿīn-i-Mubīn (1919), Fauz-i-Mubin (1920), al-Kalimah al-Mulhamah (1920), and Nuzūl-i-Āyāt-i-Furqān (1921).
claims.uncertainty: The article's list is one secondary account; title forms and dates require verification against first editions and catalogues. The date of Fauz-i-Mubin conflicts with the 2005 English edition's introductory matter.

claims.text: Siddiqui reports that a 1919 planetary-alignment prediction was narrated to Ahmad Raza Khan and prompted works on Earth's motion; the cited newspaper reports were not independently consulted.
claims.uncertainty: The contemporaneous newspapers and original 1919 text have not been independently checked.

claims.text: Siddiqui lists Fauz-i-Mubin as 1920, while a 2005 English edition's introductory matter gives 1919; the first-edition date is unresolved.
claims.locator: Siddiqui, p. 63; 2005 English edition, introductory matter, printed p. 4
claims.uncertainty: Neither source is the inspected Urdu first-edition imprint; composition and publication dates may differ.

claims.text: Siddiqui quotes a translated preface in which the work's author states a total of 105 arguments arranged in groups of 12, 50, and 43.
claims.locator: Siddiqui, pp. 67–68; quoted from Raza 2005, pp. 8–9
claims.uncertainty: The preface has not been checked in Urdu; this records the author's stated organization, not the validity or originality of the arguments.

claims.text: Siddiqui reproduces a translated geometric argument in which equal line segments and distance comparisons are used to support a physical conclusion against Earth's motion.
claims.uncertainty: No direct Urdu collation, diagram reconstruction, independent proof check, or physical validation has been performed.

claims.text: The present dossier documents historical arguments and does not present the treatise's stationary-Earth conclusion or its author's claims of proof as findings of modern astronomy.
claims.locator: Scope and limitations of this dossier; compare Siddiqui pp. 69–70 and the 2005 edition's introductory claims
claims.uncertainty: A full scientific-historical evaluation would require expert review of the original mathematical reasoning; the historical conclusion is not adopted as current science.

investigations.title: Education, fatwa-writing, Qadiri affiliation, and major works
investigations.historicalProblem: What can current academic studies establish about Khan’s education, scholarly practice, spiritual affiliation, institutional activity, and selected major works without treating devotional stories or later work counts as verified facts?
investigations.historicalContext: Ahmad Riza Khan worked in late-nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century North India. Sanyal’s 1998 article and 2005 monograph place him among the ulama of Bareilly and the Ahl-e Sunnat movement, and describe a scholarly career spanning legal responsa, Sufi leadership, institutional activity, Qur’an translation, and separate astronomy-related writings.
investigations.method: Compared relevant portions of Sanyal’s 1998 peer-reviewed article (pp. 636–637, 645) and monograph (chapter 3, pp. 51–77; madrasa discussion p. 113). Claims are attributed to those secondary works, and the monograph’s use of later biographical narratives is disclosed. No Urdu primary biography, first-edition title page, manuscript, or original passage was collated. A prefatory first-person passage in the Fatawa collection was also read through searchable digital text and compared with a separate online transcription; the year numeral differs (PDF OCR 1282; transcription 1286), and the page image remains unchecked.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: This is a source comparison and chronology, not a mathematical reconstruction. Years are retained at the precision given by Sanyal; the 1905–06 pilgrimage remains an interval. The first-person preface says his father appointed him to issue fatwas while he was under fourteen, gives his birth as 10 Shawwal 1272 AH, and says he began issuing opinions; the exact appointment year cannot be transcribed confidently because digital text witnesses differ.
investigations.reportedResult: The sources support a fuller draft outline of Khan’s training, fatwa practice, Qadiri affiliation, travel, school foundation, and selected works. They do not establish a complete bibliography or validate claims made in the astronomy treatises. A first-person prefatory report narrows the early fatwa chronology, while its year numeral remains unverified.
investigations.whatWasNew: No priority, scientific correctness, or exhaustive-work-count claim is made. The source comparison adds a distinction between the 1911 publication of Kanz al-Iman and the later editorial history of the Fatawa-e Rizwiyya collection.
investigations.limitations: The monograph is secondary and its biographical anecdotes sometimes cite Zafar ud-Din Bihari; that Urdu biography was not consulted. Primary editions of Kanz al-Iman and Fatawa-e Rizwiyya were not inspected. This dossier’s online scan was consulted for selected chapters, not read cover to cover. The prefatory page image has not been visually collated; one PDF OCR extraction and one HTML transcription disagree on whether the year is 1282 or 1286 AH. The account is retrospective even though it is first-person.
investigations.laterInfluence: Sanyal describes the later collection and publication of Khan’s writings by his family and followers; this batch does not trace subsequent reception or circulation.

claims.text: Sanyal identifies Naqi Ali Khan as Ahmad Riza’s most important teacher and says he studied the Dars-i Nizami syllabus at home, inheriting his father’s rational-sciences tradition.
claims.uncertainty: The account is secondary; it does not supply a complete class-by-class curriculum or a primary teaching certificate.

claims.text: Sanyal reports that after completing his studies at about fourteen, Khan’s father entrusted him with writing fatwas; by the 1880s he was known as a mufti and responded to questions from Bareilly and farther away.
claims.uncertainty: The age-fourteen episode is mediated through Bihari’s later biography; the 1998 article independently supports fatwa-writing’s centrality but not that precise age.

claims.text: Sanyal dates Khan’s Qadiri discipleship to Shah Al-e Rasul of Marehra to 1877 and says Nuri Miyan later guided his spiritual development.
claims.uncertainty: The relationship is recorded through secondary scholarship; no initiation document was examined.

claims.text: Sanyal reports that Ahmad Riza and his father undertook pilgrimage to Mecca in 1878.
claims.uncertainty: No itinerary or contemporary travel record was checked.

claims.text: Sanyal recounts that at the October 1900 Ahl-e Sunnat meeting in Patna a speaker called Khan the mujaddid of the current Islamic century and that the gathering was said to concur.
claims.uncertainty: This is a movement honorific reported through later biography, not an independent assessment or universally accepted title.

claims.text: Sanyal identifies Madrasa Manzar al-Islam in Bareilly as founded by Ahmad Riza in 1904; her 1998 article independently notes a Bareilly madrasa founded in that year.
claims.uncertainty: Institutional records and the first prospectus were not consulted.

claims.text: Sanyal records a second pilgrimage to Mecca and Medina in 1905–06 and discusses legal opinions written during the visit.
claims.uncertainty: The source gives a two-year interval; exact departure and return dates remain unknown.

claims.text: Sanyal reports that Khan’s Urdu Qur’an translation, Kanz al-Iman fi Tarjuma(t) al-Qur’an, was published in Muradabad in 1911; her later Encyclopaedia of the Qur’an entry also gives Muradabad 1911 and lists a 1911 edition.
claims.locator: Sanyal, monograph p. 77; “Ahmad Rida Khan,” pp. 203–204
claims.uncertainty: Both scholarly references are by Usha Sanyal, so they are not independent corroboration. The original edition title page and a specific first-edition catalogue record remain uninspected; community listings give conflicting 1910/1912 dates and title-form variation.

claims.text: Sanyal describes Fatawa-e Rizwiyya as a later collection containing many, but not all, of Khan’s legal opinions; she says only two appear to have been published in his lifetime and notes damage to manuscripts during later editorial work.
claims.uncertainty: Volume title pages, contents, manuscript witnesses, and publication chronology were not independently collated.

claims.text: In a first-person preface to the later Fatawa collection, Ahmad Riza Khan says his father appointed him to issue fatwas on 14 Shaʿban while he was not yet fourteen; he says he then began issuing opinions and his father corrected his errors. The searchable PDF text prints 1282 AH but spells the year with “eighty-six”; a separate transcription reads 1286 AH.
claims.locator: Vol. 1, part A, prefatory text, viewer text p. 94/590; online transcription entries #17228–17229
claims.uncertainty: This is a retrospective authorial statement preserved in a later edition. The digital numeral conflicts with the number spelled out in words, and the page image has not been checked; no exact year/day conversion is asserted.

investigations.title: Reported manuscript inventory of mathematical and related works
investigations.field: History of mathematics, astronomy, and manuscript bibliography
investigations.historicalProblem: What titles and dates does one secondary Arabic biographical inventory report, and what can be safely inferred before its manuscript images are inspected?
investigations.historicalContext: The online Arabic study identifies a section as manuscripts of Ahmad Riza Khan and says the author held images of about 100 manuscripts. It then lists twenty items said to concern rational sciences. The list is reproduced through a community forum rather than a manuscript catalogue.
investigations.method: Read the inventory entries and a later sample-manuscript list in the same article. Titles and dates were recorded as leads; transliterations are provisional. No manuscript image or shelfmark was accessible, and no title was translated into a technical conclusion.
investigations.observationsOrCalculations: The inventory lists twenty entries dated 1296–1336 AH (reported as 1878–1917 CE). One date inconsistency was found: the same article pairs 1296 AH with 1878 CE in the inventory and with 1828 CE in a later sample caption for the same title.
investigations.reportedResult: The source provides twenty candidate manuscript titles, including works whose titles mention circles, calendars, stars, time, and calculation. These records establish what this secondary inventory reports, not the manuscripts’ authorship, dates, contents, or scientific validity.
investigations.whatWasNew: A structured, explicitly provisional bibliography lead list was added to the research dossier, and an internal date-conversion conflict was flagged instead of silently normalizing it.
investigations.limitations: The forum repost is secondary and devotional in context; inventory images, shelfmarks, full bibliographic apparatus, and the listed manuscripts were not checked. Several transliterations may reflect online text/OCR errors. No priority, correctness, completeness, or contribution claim is made.

claims.text: Muhammad Masud Ahmad’s Arabic biographical study reports twenty manuscript titles under a section headed “Manuscripts of Ahmad Riza” and says the author held images of about 100 manuscripts.
claims.uncertainty: The online repost has no shelfmarks or linked images for these twenty entries; the count and attributions are reported by one secondary source only.

claims.text: The same article gives two incompatible Gregorian equivalents for the date 1296 AH attached to Aṭāʾib al-Iksīr: 1878 in its list and 1828 in a later sample caption.
claims.locator: Manuscripts list, item 1; later sample list, item 9
claims.uncertainty: This establishes an internal inconsistency in the consulted repost only; it does not establish the manuscript’s true date.

claims.text: The Arabic biographical study cites Maʿārif Raza (Karachi, 1983), pp. 163–223, reports a handwritten copy attributed to Ahmad Riza Khan in the author’s Karachi library, and says the treatise was printed and published in Bareilly.
claims.uncertainty: The cited issue, manuscript, Bareilly edition, publication date, and printer were not inspected; the report does not provide a shelfmark.

claims.text: The Arabic biography’s later sample list labels the al-Burhān al-Qawīm manuscript Arabic, while Alahazrat Network labels the work Persian.
claims.locator: Arabic study, manuscript sample p. 106; Alahazrat Network work page
claims.uncertainty: This records disagreement between two community-hosted descriptions, not the language of an inspected witness or edition.

claims.text: The Arabic biographical study has a separate manuscript-samples section listing eighteen items with selected language, handwriting, subject, or printed-page details; some overlap with its twenty-title inventory.
claims.uncertainty: The forum repost transmits descriptions, not the manuscript images themselves; handwriting, identity, and listed languages remain reports until the cited pages/witnesses are inspected.

openQuestions: Collate the passages in Zafar ud-Din Bihari’s Urdu biography and other early records that Sanyal cites; verify age-fourteen fatwa-writing, 1877 discipleship, 1878 pilgrimage, and the 1900 Patna episode.

Inspect the cited manuscript image and the 2005 Qibla Numa scan; collate title, script, date and folios. The reported 1324 AH / 1906 date is a secondary-list lead, not yet an independently verified manuscript or publication date.

Locate and inspect Maʿārif Raza (Karachi, 1983), pp. 163–223, and the manuscript copy reported in the author’s Karachi library; identify the Bareilly edition’s title page and resolve the reported Arabic/Persian language conflict.

Inspect the Arabic biographical study’s sample pages 95–119 and the cited manuscript images; verify which descriptions refer to the same witness, distinguish authorial handwriting from a copy made by another person, and record shelfmarks.

Inspect a copy of the earliest Kanz al-Iman edition and its title page/colophon to confirm date, title form, place, printer, collaborators, and whether any commentary accompanied it. Sanyal’s 2005 monograph and her Encyclopaedia of the Qur’an entry both report Muradabad 1911, but they share an author and do not replace primary-edition inspection; community listings give 1910 or 1912.

Map the Fatawa-e Rizwiyya volume history using title pages, contents, surviving manuscripts, and library catalogues; Rekhta now identifies one 1994 volume-12 edition, but the complete sequence and editorial history remain to be checked.
Locate the New York Times, Marlborough Express, Pittsburgh Press and Puke Times reports cited by Siddiqui; determine what Porta actually predicted and distinguish report date from event date.
Reconstruct the geometric argument and verify its translation, diagram, Euclidean references, premises, and inference with a history-of-mathematics reviewer.
Survey the four related astronomy texts and other mathematical/timekeeping writings through library catalogues and original editions; do not rely on devotional work-count websites.
Commission human review of Urdu-English translation and transliteration before publishing any direct quotation or detailed method reconstruction.

Visually inspect the prefatory page of Fatawa-e Rizwiyya vol. 1A (viewer text p. 94/590) to resolve whether the appointment-year numeral reads 1282 or 1286 AH; separately locate and collate the 14 Shaʿban 1336 letter that retrospectively states fifty years of fatwa-writing.
